---

**Proof.**

We must show $\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\log\binom{n}{pn}=H(p)$ for every $0\le p\le 1$.

**Boundary cases $p\in\{0,1\}$.** If $p=0$, then $\binom{n}{0}=1$, so $\frac1n\log\binom{n}{0}=0$, and $H(0)=-0\log 0-(1)\log 1=0$ (using $0\log 0:=0$). Likewise $p=1$ gives $\binom{n}{n}=1$ and $H(1)=0$. So the claim holds at the endpoints.

**Interior case $0<p<1$.** Set $k_n:=\lfloor pn\rfloor$; since $k_n/n\to p$ and the argument is continuous in the ratio, it suffices to work with $k=pn$ (taking $pn$ integer for notational clarity; the floor changes $\log\binom{n}{k}$ by $O(\log n)=o(n)$, hence $\frac1n$-negligibly).

Stirling's approximation in logarithmic form states, for every $m\to\infty$,
$$\log m! \;=\; m\log m - m + \tfrac12\log(2\pi m)+o(1).$$

Apply this to $n$, $pn$, and $(1-p)n$ (all $\to\infty$ since $0<p<1$):
$$\log\binom{n}{pn}=\log n!-\log(pn)!-\log((1-p)n)!.$$

Substituting and collecting the **linear** terms $(-n)+pn+(1-p)n=0$, and the **leading logarithmic** terms:
$$n\log n - pn\log(pn)-(1-p)n\log((1-p)n).$$
Writing $\log(pn)=\log p+\log n$ and $\log((1-p)n)=\log(1-p)+\log n$,
$$n\log n - pn\log p - pn\log n - (1-p)n\log(1-p)-(1-p)n\log n$$
$$=\;n\log n\bigl(1-p-(1-p)\bigr)-pn\log p-(1-p)n\log(1-p)$$
$$=\;-pn\log p-(1-p)n\log(1-p)\;=\;nH(p).$$

The **subleading** terms are the half-logarithms:
$$\tfrac12\Bigl[\log(2\pi n)-\log(2\pi pn)-\log\bigl(2\pi(1-p)n\bigr)\Bigr]
=\tfrac12\log\frac{2\pi n}{(2\pi)^2\,p(1-p)\,n^2}
=-\tfrac12\log\bigl(2\pi n\,p(1-p)\bigr),$$
which is $O(\log n)=o(n)$. The $o(1)$ remainders from Stirling are also $o(n)$.

Therefore
$$\log\binom{n}{pn}=nH(p)+o(n),$$
and dividing by $n$,
$$\frac1n\log\binom{n}{pn}=H(p)+o(1)\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}H(p).$$

Combining with the verified boundary cases, the limit holds for all $0\le p\le 1$. $\blacksquare$
